title: Poems: Forms and Feelings
theme: Poetry: forms, sound and emotional effect
objectives: I can name poetic forms and tools (sonnet, ballad, elegy, lyric, meter) and explain what each one does.
I can describe the effect of a poem using words such as haunting, stark, and poignant.
I can explain how a speaker's sentiment shows in word choice and rhythm.
I can write a short response to a poem using at least three words from this unit.
rationale: Grade 7 poetry analysis needs two kinds of words. Four terms name a poem's forms and measures (sonnet, ballad, elegy, meter) and one names a voice (lyric), so students can say what kind of poem they are reading. The rest describe a poem's feeling and effect (sentiment, haunting, stark, poignant) and the act of reading closely (contemplate). Students practice with a narrative about a class poetry unit so that the forms are shown in use before they meet real poems. Monologue, omniscient, intimate, and wistful return from the point-of-view and tone units so that students can describe a poem's speaker as well as its form.

words.def: A poem of fourteen lines that follows a set pattern of rhyme.
words.ex: Shakespeare wrote many sonnets, and each one has fourteen lines.
words.ex2: The class wrote a sonnet about the first snowfall, counting each line to make sure it reached fourteen.
words.nonExample: A short poem of only four lines is not a sonnet.

apps.academic: In English class, we compared how two poets turned their ideas in a sonnet.
apps.spoken: I'm trying to write a sonnet, but fourteen rhyming lines is hard.
apps.writing: Use sonnet for a poem with fourteen lines and a rhyme pattern.

misuse.s: A sonnet is a long story poem that can run for hundreds of lines.

words.def: A poem or song that tells a story, usually in short verses.

words.ex2: Folk singers passed the ballad from village to village long before it was written down.

apps.writing: Use ballad for a poem or song that tells a story.

words.def: A poem of sorrow that mourns someone who has died.

words.ex2: Her elegy for the old oak tree praised its shade and mourned its fall.

words.def: The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables that gives a poem its rhythm.
words.ex: The poem's steady meter made it feel like a heartbeat.
words.ex2: Clap the meter of each line to find where the stresses fall.
words.nonExample: The number of pages in a book of poems is not its meter.

apps.spoken: Say it aloud and tap the meter with your finger.
apps.writing: Use meter for the pattern of beats in a line of verse, not for a measuring tool.

words.def: Expressing a speaker's personal feelings in a musical, song-like way.

words.ex2: Her lyric style made even plain words sound like part of a song.
words.nonExample: A poem that tells a long story about a battle is narrative, not lyric.

apps.academic: A lyric poem usually has one speaker who shares a thought or a feeling.
apps.spoken: That song has such lyric beauty; it makes me feel calm.
apps.writing: Use lyric for poems of personal feeling and for writing with a song-like sound.

cloze2.s: The ___ lines of the poem were short and musical, like the words of a song.

words.def: A feeling or opinion, especially one that is expressed in words.
words.ex: The card expressed a warm sentiment of thanks to the teacher.
words.ex2: Public sentiment turned against the plan after its cost became clear.
words.nonExample: A list of numbers expresses no sentiment at all.

apps.writing: Use sentiment for a feeling or opinion stated in words.

cloze.s: The poem's closing ___ was simple: gratitude for everything the grandmother had given.

misuse.s: The sentiment was a cold, empty list of facts with no feeling or opinion in it.

words.def: Beautiful or sad in a way that stays in your mind long afterward.
words.ex: The singer's haunting melody echoed in my head all night.
words.ex2: The photograph of the empty playground was haunting.
words.nonExample: A forgettable song you stop thinking about as soon as it ends is not haunting.

apps.academic: Critics called the poem's last image haunting because it lingers after the words end.
apps.spoken: That song is haunting; I can't stop humming it.
apps.writing: Use haunting for an image or sound that stays in the mind, beautiful or sad.

cloze2.s: A ___ violin tune drifted across the quiet lake at dusk and lingered long after it stopped.

misuse.s: The haunting song was so forgettable that no one remembered it a minute later.
misuse.why: Haunting means it stays in your mind; a song nobody remembers is the opposite.

words.frame: A haunting image stays in my mind because ___.

words.def: Plain, bare, and harsh, with nothing to soften it.
words.ex: The stark white walls of the empty room made her feel even more alone.
words.ex2: The poet used stark language, short plain words with no decoration, to describe the storm's damage.
words.nonExample: A cozy room filled with rugs, pillows, and soft lamps is not stark.

apps.academic: The poem's stark images, a bare tree and an empty road, create a lonely mood.
apps.spoken: The room was so stark that it felt cold.
apps.writing: Use stark for scenes or language that are bare and harsh, with no softening.

cloze2.s: The report gave a ___ description of the flood damage, listing every loss without comfort or decoration.

words.def: To think about something deeply and for a long time.
words.ex: She sat on the dock to contemplate her choices before making the big decision.
words.ex2: The poet liked to contemplate the sea before writing a single line.
words.nonExample: Glancing at a sign and moving on is not contemplating it.

apps.academic: Before you write about a poem, contemplate what the speaker wants the reader to feel.
apps.spoken: I need some quiet time to contemplate this.
apps.writing: Use contemplate for long, serious thought, not a quick look.

words.def: Causing a deep feeling of sadness or tender emotion.
words.ex: The poignant letter from the soldier's mother made the whole class go quiet.
words.ex2: It was poignant to see the old teacher visit her first classroom again.
words.nonExample: A funny joke that makes everyone laugh is not poignant.

apps.academic: The poem is poignant because it joins happy memories with the sadness of loss.
apps.spoken: That scene was so poignant that I teared up.
apps.writing: Use poignant for moments that touch the heart with sadness or tenderness.

cloze.s: The ___ ending of the film, in which two old friends said goodbye, left many viewers in tears.

cloze2.s: The poem was ___ because it described a happy memory that could never come back.

passage.title: A Poem That Sounded Like Music
paras: In Ms. Park's poetry unit, Elias began with a fear: he thought poems were puzzles with hidden answers. On the first day she wrote a line on the board and asked the class to read it aloud twice. "Hear the beat?" she said. "That pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables is the poem's meter." Elias tapped it on his desk, and for the first time, poetry sounded like music.

Over three weeks the class met the forms. A sonnet, Ms. Park explained, has fourteen lines and usually turns a corner partway through, as if the speaker changes his mind. A ballad tells a story, often about love, danger, or a hero, and it was traditionally sung. An elegy mourns someone who has died, though it can also honor what the person meant. Elias liked the ballad best, because he could hear a tale unfolding line by line.

Then the class read a lyric poem, a short piece in which one speaker shares personal feelings. It described a grandmother's empty kitchen at dusk. "What sentiment does the speaker feel?" Ms. Park asked. "Sadness," Rosa answered. "Or maybe a tender memory." Elias noticed the poet's word choice: the kitchen light was stark, the white walls bare and bright with nothing to soften them, and the silence seemed haunting, as if the memories lingered in the room.

For his own poem, Elias decided to contemplate what he missed most about last spring. He sat by the window for an hour, saying nothing and letting images drift in. The result was an elegy for his dog, Pepper, who had died in March. "It is the most poignant poem in the class," Ms. Park said quietly after reading it, "because the sadness is real and the memories are happy."

On the last day, Elias read his poem aloud. He tapped the meter on his desk, just as he had learned, and the room went still. When he finished, Rosa wiped her eyes, and someone clapped softly. Poetry was no longer a puzzle. It was a way to say what was too large for plain sentences.

constructed.prompt: A friend wants to write a poem about a brave rescue and another about a quiet snowfall. Say which form fits each, using sonnet and ballad.
look: matches the story poem to a ballad
gives a reason for the sonnet choice
constructed.model: The rescue fits a ballad because a ballad tells a story. The quiet snowfall could be a sonnet, because a fourteen-line form helps the poet focus on one image and one feeling.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for reading and describing poems, read a narrative about a class poetry unit, practice word families, and write short responses that name forms and effects. The words let students say what kind of poem they are reading, how it sounds, and how it feels.

notes.va.sonnet.n: Teach by counting lines. Show a rhyming example and have students mark the pattern with letters. Do not require students to memorize Shakespearean or Petrarchan variants; a fourteen-line rhymed poem is enough for this grade.
notes.va.ballad.n: Contrast with lyric: a ballad has a plot and characters. Have students retell a ballad in three sentences. Spanish balada can also name a romantic song, so check meaning in the language of origin.
notes.va.elegy.n: A sensitive word for students who have lost someone; offer a choice of subject (a pet, a place, a time). Elegy mourns but can also comfort. Pair with poignant to talk about tone.
notes.va.meter.n: Tier 3 and multiple-meaning: in science and math, meter also means a unit of length, which students know. Keep this sense to the pattern of beats in a line and let students tap the beat. Marking stressed syllables with a slash is enough.
notes.va.lyric.adj: Distinguish lyric (a speaker's feeling) from narrative (a story). Link to song lyrics. The family words lyrics, lyrical, and lyricist show a noun, an adjective, and a person word.
notes.va.sentiment.n: Students may know sentimental; show that sentiment is a plain noun for a feeling or opinion. Ask what sentiment the speaker expresses, and point to words that show it.
notes.va.haunting.adj: A figurative adjective: nothing is literally haunting the reader. Ask students to name an image or a sound that stayed with them. Keep it separate from haunted (a place with ghosts).
notes.va.stark.adj: Used for bare scenes and plain language. Students may know stark in stark contrast; show that the root idea is bare and harsh. Link to word choice: short, plain words can be stark too.
notes.va.contemplate.v: A slow, quiet word; model it by silently looking at a picture for a full minute and then writing about it. Contrast with look at and glance.
notes.va.poignant.adj: Often mispronounced; practice POYN-yunt. Emphasize that poignant mixes sadness with tenderness. Use a short passage or a photo and ask students to explain what makes it poignant.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The poem tells what happens to a sailor who never returns, and it has short, singable verses. That is a ballad. The last two lines stay with me after I stop reading, so I would call them haunting. I will use ballad for the form and haunting for the effect.'

misconceptions: A sonnet can have any number of lines.
A ballad is a slow love song.

extend: Write a four-line ballad that tells a small story and tap its meter.

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit sonnet/ballad/elegy as a sort after two days and again at one week. Ask students to use monologue, omniscient, intimate, and wistful to describe a poem's speaker or mood, and to connect poignant and haunting with tone words from the first unit.

frames: A ___ tells a story, but a ___ shares a feeling.
The image of ___ is haunting because ___.
wida.oral: Partner A reads a short poem or song line aloud and taps the meter; Partner B names the form or the effect (such as haunting or poignant) and explains why.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (balada, métrica, inolvidable, austero, conmovedor, contemplar) not reviewed by a native speaker; balada has a second everyday sense and métrica should be checked for verse meter.

Fact claims: a sonnet has fourteen lines; Shakespeare wrote many sonnets; a ballad tells a story and was traditionally sung; an elegy mourns the dead; meter is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Confirm wording against a literary-terms reference.
Sense boundaries: meter (unit of length) and stark (stark contrast) have other uses that are not taught here.
